assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable light-matter coupling possible on a chip, with dispersive readout and quantum-limited microwave measurement and control. It is the working interface of essentially every superconducting quantum processor and also launched microwave quantum optics with artificial atoms. It opened a regime (strong coupling with engineered, tunable atoms and resonators) that was not previously accessible, and it is a clear case of a basic quantum phenomenon made visible and controllable.
assessment.attribution: The theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf, 2004) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf et al., 2004) form a natural pairing of theory and experiment, so a three-person prize is plausible. Yale and ETH experiments and the theory were closely intertwined; Girvin's role and the earlier Cooper-pair-box groups are not in the supplied credit, so the configuration may be contested.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of reproduction across many laboratories and platforms; the physics is stable and the interpretation is not in doubt. Recognition is timely, especially following the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which supplies the platform on which cQED builds. I should note my field proximity to this subject and weigh it cautiously.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would view cQED as sufficiently distinct from the 2025 circuit-tunnelling prize or as a natural continuation.
Exact allocation of credit between the theory proposal and the first experiments, and omission of other key contributors from the credited names.
My own closeness to this community may bias my view of its significance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal showed how to perform quantum logic with trapped ions, and Blatt's group and others turned it into working gates, entanglement and algorithms. It is a foundational demonstration that controlled quantum computation is physically possible, with exceptional gate fidelities and long coherence.
assessment.attribution: A theory pair plus a leading experimentalist is a natural configuration. Wineland's earlier work (2012 prize) and contributions of other ion-trap groups (e.g. Innsbruck vs. NIST vs. Oxford, Maryland) complicate the story, and the supplied names do not include them.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years since the 1995 proposal, with extensive independent confirmation and commercial systems. It is mature, though some of the credit overlaps with the 2012 prize. The recognition would be timely if the committee wants to honour quantum-computing hardware beyond superconducting circuits.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche and how much of the contribution is regarded as new.
Ballot B044 contains the same names under a broader description, so the committee must consider which framing is right.
I am not an ion-trap specialist and defer on the relative importance of different ion-trap groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction established that fragile quantum information can be protected in principle, and the threshold theorem made scalable quantum computing a conceptual possibility. Kitaev's topological codes also connected information theory to condensed-matter physics. The importance is high, and experiments with logical qubits below threshold are now appearing.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane gave the first codes, Kitaev the fault-tolerance and topological ideas, but Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or and others also made decisive contributions. A three-person selection from the supplied names is possible but unavoidably omits significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: The theory is mature and stable. Experimental confirmation is recent and still developing: below-threshold surface-code memories exist, but large-scale fault-tolerant computing has not been demonstrated. The Nobel criterion of a discovery of nature, rather than a mathematical construction, makes timing somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Whether the prize committee regards this theoretical work as physics discovery or as information theory.
Unresolved credit among many contributors beyond the three names.
Fault-tolerant computation at scale is still ahead of us, so experimental validation is incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-state cooling and quantum control of mechanical oscillators, including entanglement and non-classical states of massive objects, extend quantum physics to a new regime of macroscopic matter. The Cleland group's quantum state of a mechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit and Teufel's sideband cooling and squeezing of motion are clear, clean experiments. Kippenberg's work on cavity optomechanics adds important breadth.
assessment.attribution: Five names are credited, and a fair prize configuration must be chosen carefully among Aspelmeyer, Cleland, Kippenberg, Painter and Teufel. The decisive first quantum-ground-state demonstrations (Cleland, then Teufel and Painter in 2011) are close in time. I propose Cleland, Teufel and Kippenberg as a defensible subset, but the choice is genuinely contested.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in several platforms (electromechanical, optomechanical, phononic) over fifteen years. Applications such as sensing and quantum transduction are still developing, so the fundamental discovery is more mature than the technology.
uncertainties: Five credible contributors cannot all be recognised, and the choice among Aspelmeyer, Painter, Teufel, Cleland and Kippenberg is difficult.
Whether the committee sees this as a single discovery or as a collection of related advances.
Overlap with the 2025 prize theme of macroscopic quantum phenomena in circuits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of individually trapped Rydberg atoms have turned neutral atoms into a platform for quantum simulation and gate-based computation, with demonstrations of many-body phases, entanglement and error-corrected logical operations. The enabling ideas include Rydberg blockade for quantum gates and optical tweezer arrays.
assessment.attribution: The Rydberg-blockade gate proposal (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller, Lukin et al., 2000) and the experimental platforms (Browaeys, Lukin, Saffman, Bernien, Endres and others) have complicated authorship. The supplied credit has four names, and Zoller's contribution overlaps with other ballots. My subset favours experimental demonstrations.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing, with independent confirmation by several groups, but the field is still moving quickly and the long-term interpretation of its significance may change. Possibly somewhat premature relative to more established candidates.
uncertainties: Fast-moving field in which the most important results may still lie ahead.
Credit split between theory proposals and the experimental realisations.
I defer to colleagues in atomic physics on the relative merits of the experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Semiconductor quantum-dot spin qubits demonstrate coherent control of single electron spins in solid-state devices, beginning with the Loss-DiVincenzo proposal. Single and two-qubit gates, readout and, recently, silicon qubits with high fidelity show a path to scalable devices compatible with existing manufacturing. Important, but the fundamental discovery aspect is less singular than for some others.
assessment.attribution: Loss (and DiVincenzo, who is not in the supplied names) for the proposal; Tarucha, Vandersypen, and Marcus for experimental demonstrations in GaAs and silicon. Four names are listed, and the choice of three means leaving out an important contributor. Marcus has strong claims for the early GaAs coherent control and I would not consider the choice settled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by multiple laboratories; however, the platform has not yet shown the scale of competing technologies, and its eventual role is uncertain. Recognition could come at a later date without loss.
uncertainties: DiVincenzo's contribution to the proposal is not covered by the supplied credit.
Whether the platform will remain competitive with superconducting and ion-based approaches.
Difficulty of distinguishing among Marcus, Tarucha and Vandersypen.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea and developed by Ye into clocks with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level, is a landmark in precision measurement. It enables tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The physics is clean, and every physical detail of the systematic effects has been controlled.
assessment.attribution: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, Ye for the realisation of record accuracy and many-body clock physics. A two-person prize is natural. Contributions of other groups (e.g. at PTB, NIST, SYRTE) and the overlap with Hall's 2005 work on frequency combs could be raised.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed and stable. Timing is right, though a redefinition of the second has not yet taken place and some might prefer to wait for that.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a physics discovery or as an instrument and metrology achievement.
Overlap with prior prizes in frequency metrology and optical clocks (Hall, Hänsch 2005; Wineland 2012).
I am less expert in atomic clocks and defer to colleagues on the relative importance of competing clock approaches.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) turned entanglement and the no-cloning principle into a cryptographic protocol, and experimental demonstrations including satellite-based links brought it to global scale. It is a conceptually clear and lasting application of quantum foundations, complementary to the 2022 prize on entangled-photon tests of Bell inequalities.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard for BB84 and Ekert for the entanglement-based protocol give a natural trio from the credited names. Jian-Wei Pan is the leading experimentalist for networks, and an experiment-oriented prize could take a different configuration. Wiesner's earlier conjugate coding is outside the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The protocols are decades old and widely validated; practical security and the scalability of global networks are still developing, and the discovery is as much a protocol as a physical phenomenon. Recognition is timely but the weight of the physics discovery is lower than that of the candidates above.
uncertainties: Whether this should be viewed as physics or as an information-theoretic invention, and how to weigh the practical status of QKD.
The choice between a theory-oriented and an experiment-oriented trio given four credited names.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on quantum information science.
